subject: How to combine different areal geometries

messages.author: f9c6a2087c744460
messages.subject: How to combine different areal geometries
parts:
Hi all,

First this is not so much a coding question, but a 'how do I approach this problem' question. I hope this is in keeping with the question guidelines for the group.

Data: I am working with disease incidence data and I have a list of cases collected over 20 years or so each of which are geocoded. I also have census data for over 18000 administrative small areas. Using this I have counted observed and calculated expected cases per area and implemented the BYM model (so far a spatial analysis only). I also have available Corine land usage maps for several years over the 20 year period - and one year prior to the 20 year period. These maps are also areal data with about 20,000 areas each, although the boundaries are different to the administrative areas , and also the boundaries are different for Corine maps in different years (as the land use has changed in that time). (I do also have other data in point form such as social mineral levels that I might later want to add in - but for now I'm not worry about that).

I would like to construct an INLA model that would assist me to answer the question: "is land use associated with disease incidence" - and since the land use has changed over time, I guess this needs to be a space-time model. This is as far as I can get before becoming confused.

I understand the maths well enough to have implemented an OpenBugs and INLA areal  BYM model with areal covariates such as population density for each areal unit, but beyond that I get stuck (I found the advanced parts of the INLA course hard to follow). I believe that to answer this question I probably need to implement an SPDE approach, but I realise that means representing my data in point form and building a MESH and stack. Is this the correct approach ? I struggle with the idea of representing some of the areal data as point data - particularly for land use, which is by nature very discrete data. Conceptually I have difficulty with the idea of representing discrete data by points on continuous field - although I accept this may be my own lack of understanding. When it comes to disease risk, I can accept this is a continuous field, however I don't know how to represent observed and expected cases as point data in a MESH model (and note that in many cases the observed cases = 0 ).

Can anyone point me in the right direction here? Again apologies if this is not the right sort of question for the forum.
I have the Blangiardo and Cameletti book on order but it will take a while to arrive in I believe.

Many thanks,
James

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to combine different areal geometries
parts:
Hi James,

Your problem seems interesting. Let me try to check if I understood it.

First point: When you say that land use is discrete data (changes not
smooth over space and time), it may does not mean that you cannot have
it at the individual locations. You can extract the land use for each
disease case, over space-time. The same for the covariates at census
areas level. So, you can have the covariates everywhere, particularly at
the space-time points where you have the incidence data. Do you agree
with this? Maybe I misunderstood the problem.

Second point: I didn't understood your incidence data, because you
mention about zeros... If you have a case-control study, then you may
use a Binomial (maybe any zero-inflated) likelihood. But, if you only
have the incidence data and you need to use population data (from
census), the problem is trick...

Elias

messages.author: f66907f526d3c7bf
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to combine different areal geometries
parts:
Hi!

For the modelling, have a look at chapter 6 of Banerjee Carlin &
Gelfand (2004) Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data. If
I understand your problem, you have 2 maps which each partition the
region - one administrative and one from Corine - incidence data for
one and the other is a covariate in the model.

The BCG approach is to make a new partition by overlaying the two maps
to create a new one simply by merging the lines. Each administrative
polygon is then made up of several land use polygons ("atoms"). If the
expected disease incidence in each atom is lambda, then the incidence
in the administrative region is the sum of the lambdas, and the number
of cases follows a Poisson distribution with mean equal to this sum.

I had a slightly similar problem last year, and I don't think INLA can
deal this, because your likelihood is of the form

X ~ Po(sum \lambda) = Po(sum exp(sum \beta X))

which will look horrible.

I don't know if you could do some imputation. Given a count N in an
administrative region, the number of cases in each atom is
multinomial, so you might be able to use that to simulate the cases in
each atom, fit the model, and then average (somehow) over the imputed
data.

Hopefully there's a better solution to this...

Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

Thank you for the information - I will check out that reference I don't know it.

Regarding your description of the BCG approach. I had similar thoughts myself and so used one of the Corine maps as a test. An intersection of the 18,000 administrative areas and 20,000 land use polygons took 5 days to complete in QGIS on a server and produced a map with 70,000 'atoms'. I could of course apportion case counts proportional to area per atom and then build a BYM model. However  -that is just one Corine year out of 4 and the geometries are different each time. Its not feasible to intersect them all to produce smaller and smaller 'atoms' (quarks ??? :) )as the numbers of atoms will be enormous and it will take forever.

James

parts:
On 15/10/15 16:19, jpkr...@gmail.com wrote:
> First point: Yes you are correct I could calculate each covariate for
> each case. I had not thought of that previously. I'm not sure how to
> use that to say something about incidence however ?

I didn't understood this question... without considering population at
risk (just pure point process) the problem to compute the Exposure is as
proposed in http://arxiv.org/abs/1111.0641

But, you do need to consider the population (available at census areas)
to compute Exposure. As Bob's said, it is not straightforward for INLA
to have
\lambda = exp ( sum linear predictor at some set)

Elias
